The ultimate quality of a meta-analysis depends on the quality of the primary studies on which it is based. A meta-analysis is most

of the results reported in each trial.

questions.explanation:
Student's t-test is a parametric test; it is used to test if the means of observations from two samples are signi�cantly di�erent. Wilcoxon

populations. It is a non-parametric equivalent of ANOVA while Friedman test is a non-parametric test analogous to repeated measures
ANOVA.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an agreed method of assessing quality of conducting and reporting systematic reviews and metaanalyses?
questions.explanation:
The Quality of Reporting of Meta-analyses (QUOROM) conference was convened to address standards for improving the quality of reporting
of meta-analyses of clinical randomised controlled trials (RCTs). The QUOROM group consisted of 30 clinical epidemiologists, clinicians,
statisticians, editors, and researchers. In conference, the group was asked to identify items they thought should be included in a checklist of
standards. A modi�ed Delphi technique was used in assessing candidate items. The conference resulted in the QUOROM statement, a
checklist, and a �ow diagram.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best examined antipsychotic in terms of negative symptoms of schizophrenia?

questions.question_text: Which of the following is associated with narcolepsy?
questions.explanation:
Narcolepsy is associated with cataplexy (NOT catalepsy / waxy �exibility – the latter are catatonic features). It is a disabling sleep disorder
a�ecting 0·02% of adults worldwide. It is characterised by severe, irresistible daytime sleepiness and sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy),
and can be associated with sleep-onset or sleep-o�set paralysis and hallucinations, frequent movement and awakening during sleep, and
weight gain. Sleep monitoring during night and day shows rapid sleep onset and abnormal, shortened rapid-eye-movement sleep latencies.
The onset of narcolepsy with cataplexy is usually during teenage and young adulthood and persists throughout the lifetime.
Pathophysiological studies have shown that the disease is caused by the early loss of neurons in the hypothalamus that produce hypocretin,
a wakefulness-associated neurotransmitter present in cerebrospinal �uid. The cause of neural loss could be autoimmune since most
patients (>90%) have the HLA DQB1*0602 allele that predisposes individuals to the disorder. The frequency of HLA-DR2 is also increased in
narcolepsy though not as high as HLA DQB1*0602. Treatment is with stimulant drugs to suppress daytime sleepiness, antidepressants for
cataplexy, and ? hydroxybutyrate for both symptoms.

questions.question_text: Narcolepsy is characterized by all of the following except
questions.explanation:

sleepiness, sudden sleep attacks (narcolepsy) - the sleep is refreshing as it is REM in nature, cataplexy (seen in 75% of patients), sleep
paralysis (seen in 30%), hypnagogic hallucinations. Only 10% of individuals present with all four phenomena. Automatic behaviours are
reported in around one-third (complex behaviours that are not recalled when they regain alertness). The overall sleep duration per 24 hours
is NOT increased in narcolepsy due to reduced and fragmented nocturnal sleep.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be a preventative strategy to reduce the risk of schizophrenia across populations globally?

options.text: Preventing the emergence of clozapine resistance
Identi�cation of those at high risk

questions.explanation:
Mrazek and Haggerty (1994) framework for the prevention of mental disorders includes universal, selective and indicated prevention.
Universal interventions are directed to a general population group. This is largely a primary prevention. Though these are directed at the
general population who do not have speci�c risk factors, there are some epidemiological factors for schizophrenia that are so widespread
that their targeting can be considered a universal intervention. E.g. urban living, poor social capital including low social cohesion, exclusion
and discrimination, low socio-economic status, obstetric complications, illicit drug use, childhood trauma and experiencing stressful life
events. Increasing social capital, decreasing discrimination, and reducing poverty are possible goals of universal prevention. But universal
interventions are di�cult to evaluate, costly, and need large scale implementation in diseases of low incidence such as schizophrenia. Early
and e�ective interventions, rather than universal prevention strategies, are the most cost-e�ective population health strategies available.
Selective approaches are targeted at people who are at increased risk based on an understanding of the known risk factors and/or aetiology
of the disorder. Indicated approaches target high risk individuals with minimal but detectable signs or symptoms foreshadowing mental
disorder, but who do not meet diagnostic levels currently. Both selective and indicated approaches are secondary prevention methods.

questions.explanation: Premature ejaculation is the most common reported sexual disorder in men. It is a disorder of orgasmic function.

questions.question_text: The rate of spontaneous congenital malformations associated with pregnancy is
questions.explanation:
Pregnancy is associated with risk of spontaneous major malformation (2-3% of all pregnancies) and drugs account for only 5 of every 100
malformations that occur.

questions.question_text: Which of the following predicts poor treatment response in chronic fatigue syndrome when treated with CBT/graded exercise?
questions.explanation:
Predictors of poor outcome when treating CFS include (Powell et al, 2004) 1. claiming a disability related bene�t 2. low sense of control 3.
strong focus on physical symptoms 4. being passive with reduced activity and 5. membership of self help group (Note: this does not mean
that self help groups worsen CFS; membership may be an indicator of perceived severity)

questions.question_text: What is the most common presentation seen in women with postpartum psychosis?
questions.explanation:
Postpartum psychosis: An acute psychotic episode, occurring following 1.5/1000 live births, peak occurrence at 2 wks postpartum. Aetiology
is unknown, but may relate to reduction of oestrogen (leading to DA super-sensitivity), cortisol levels, or postpartum thyroiditis. Symptoms 3
common clinical presentations: prominent a�ective symptoms (80%) mania or depression with psychotic symptoms; schizophreniform
disorder (15%); acute organic psychosis (5%) Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry; 756

questions.question_text:
A bipolar patient taking lithium was recently started on SSRI. Which of the following would you suspect as serotonin syndrome rather than
lithium toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Lithium toxicity is clinically remarkably similar to serotonin syndrome. But a blood test is often helpful to clinch toxic levels. Hyperpyrexia is
seen in severe serotonin syndrome but very usual to be due to lithium toxicity per se.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a positive prognostic factor for anorexia?
questions.explanation:
Younger age of onset is a positive prognostic factor for anorexia, in terms of short term outcome. The rest of the listed are negative
prognostic factors.

questions.question_text:
A family has recently moved near a countryside school. Their 6-year-old daughter does not speak to anyone at the school in the �rst few
months of enrolment. She makes gestures when her friends are around but will not speak to them too. She has no signs of developmental
delay and speaks well at home and when examined by the psychologist. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Selective mutism is seen in school age children presenting with refusal to speak in social settings such as a classroom. The language
development may be normal. These children have a higher risk of later development of social phobia.

questions.question_text:
A 40-year-old man has had 5 depressive episodes in the past and every time following treatment of depression he had developed
hypomania. What would you prescribe?
questions.explanation:
Antidepressant-induced mania/hypomania has been reported with all major antidepressant classes in a subgroup of about 20-40% of
bipolar patients. Lithium may confer better protection against this outcome when compared with other standard mood stabilizers, although
switch rates have been reported with comparable frequencies on or o� mood stabilizers. Mood switches were less frequent in patients
receiving lithium (15%) than in patients not treated with lithium (44%) in a small naturalistic study. Risk factors for antidepressant induced
switch includes (i) previous antidepressant-induced manias, (ii) a bipolar family history, and (iii) exposure to multiple antidepressant trials
and (iv) initial illness beginning in adolescence or young adulthood. Henry C, Sorbara F, Lacoste J, Gindre C, Leboyer M. Antidepressant-
induced mania in bipolar patients: identi�cation of risk factors. J Clin Psychiatry 2001 Apr;62(4):249-55

questions.question_text: What is the most appropriate treatment for a teenager with obsessive-compulsive disorder?
questions.explanation:
1st line agents for OCD treatment are SSRIs (sertraline and �uoxetine). Results from multiple randomised placebo-controlled trials of both
medication and Cognitive-behavioural interventions in children and adolescents with OCD have con�rmed the most evidence for successful
treatment of this disorder compared to any of the other anxiety disorders of childhood. A recent multi-site National Institute of Health
funded investigation of Sertraline and cognitive-behavioural therapy each alone, and in combination for the treatment of childhood onset
OCD, the Paediatric OCD Treatment Study (POTS) revealed that the combination was superior to either treatment alone. Sertraline also has
UK license for OCD in teenagers.

questions.question_text: The rate of completed suicide in children and adolescents with bipolar disorder is
questions.explanation:
Early onset BPD has a poor outcome with 50% showing a long-term decline in function. The course is often chronic and less responsive to
treatment, with atypical and rapid-cycling features especially di�cult to treat. Suicide risk is high with rates of completed suicide
approximately 10%.

questions.question_text: What percentage of children with major depressive episode will later manifest bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation: About 20% of children and adolescents who initially show serious depression will "switch" to manic or mixed (manic-depressive) episodes.

questions.question_text: A man with Parkinson's disease develops psychotic symptoms. He has never been on antipsychotics before. The best treatment for him is:
questions.explanation:
Clozapine is the most e�ective drug for psychosis in Parkinson's disease. But the practical limitations of its use have led to trials of other
atypical antipsychotics that do not require the intensive monitoring that is necessary for clozapine. Of these, quetiapine shows the most
promise, but placebo-controlled trials are lacking. The use of olanzapine, risperidone and aripiprazole appears limited by unacceptable
motor deterioration (Samuel et al.2006). Excerpt from Samuel et al. Clinical management of Parkinson's disease dementia: pitfalls and
progress. Advan. Psychiatr. Treat. Mar 2006; 12: 121 - 129.

questions.question_text: Which antidementia drug inhibits both acetylcholinesterase and Butyl cholinesterase in the CNS?
questions.explanation:
Donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), Galantamine (Reminyl) are cholinesterase inhibitors used to treat mild to moderate cognitive
impairment in Alzheimer's disease. These drugs can be used in patients with MMSE score between 10 and 20. They act by decreasing the
inactivation Acetylcholine and, thus, potentiating the cholinergic neurotransmission. This can lead to some (but not long lasting)
improvement in memory and goal-directed thought. Donepezil is well tolerated and widely used. Rivastigmine (inhibits both acetyl and
butyrylcholinesterases) and Galantamine appear more likely to cause gastrointestinal (GI) and neuropsychiatric adverse e�ects than does
Donepezil. These medications cannot prevent the progressive neuronal degeneration seen in the disorder. Tacrine is rarely used, because of
its potential for hepatotoxicity. Memantine (Ebixa) protects neurons from excessive amounts of glutamate, which may be neurotoxic. Trials
show bene�ts of Memantine augmentation of Donepezil. Cochrane review indicates use in DAT, vascular and mixed dementias.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Y su�ers from a long-standing diagnosis of Parkinson's disease and has developed a related dementia. Which of the following drugs has
trial support for e�cacy?
questions.explanation: Rivastigmine has good evidence for treatment of Parkinson's dementia and Lewy body dementia.

questions.question_text: What is the SECOND most common cause of dementia in the under 65s?
questions.explanation:
Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia in younger people. Around one-third of younger people with dementia have
Alzheimer's disease. Vascular dementia is the second most common form of dementia in younger people. Around 20 per cent of younger
people with dementia have vascular dementia. Around 12 per cent of younger people with dementia have frontotemporal dementia (data
from alzheimers.org.uk).

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients with learning disability su�ers from a severe form of mental retardation?
questions.explanation:
Mild mental retardation (IQ range, 50 to 70) represents approximately 85 percent of persons with mental retardation. Moderate mental
retardation (IQ range, 35-50) represents about 10 percent of persons with mental retardation. Severe mental retardation (IQ range, 20-35)
comprises about 4 percent of individuals with mental retardation. Profound mental retardation (IQ range below 20) constitutes
approximately 1 to 2 percent of persons with mental retardation. Most individuals with profound mental retardation have identi�able
causes for their condition.

questions.question_text: What is the most common behavioural phenotype seen in Prader-Willi syndrome?

options.text: Increased appetite and incessant skin picking

correct_answer.text: Increased appetite and incessant skin picking

questions.explanation:
Behavioural phenotypes: Food obsession, insatiable appetite, hyperphagia, obesity, skin picking are all important behavioral phenotypes
seen in Prader-Willi syndrome.

questions.question_text: What is the prevalence of depression among individuals with intellectual disabilities?
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of depression is around 2-4%. Depressed mood and vegetative symptoms are the most striking symptoms, even though
complaints of depression are not always expressed. A depressive mood is not verbalized, particularly among individuals at a lower
intelligence level, but may well be observable.

questions.question_text: 'Hypertelorism' is a feature seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Hypertelorism refers to an abnormally increased distance between two organs or bodily parts, usually referring to an increased distance
between the orbits (eyes). It is seen in some conditions like Di George's syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Edwards syndrome, cridu-chat
syndrome and neuro�bromatosis. Salient features of DiGeorge syndrome can be summarized using the mnemonic CATCH-22, with the 22
reminding us of chromosome 22, andCATCH referring to Cardiac Abnormality, Abnormal facies (palatal abnormalities, hypertelorism),
Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia/Hypoparathyroidism.

questions.question_text: A woman was said to employ repeatedly a "neurotic defense mechanism". Which of the following is likely to be observed?
questions.explanation:
Converting unconscious impulses into their opposites, resulting in behaviour that is completely the opposite of what one feels, is called
reaction formation. It can work e�ectively for coping in the short term, but on repeated use, will produce signi�cant 'neurotic' symptoms.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements best describes the therapeutic technique of shaping?

options.text: Removing all sources of information for an allotted time
Reinforcing speci�c appropriate behaviours while ignoring inappropriate behaviours
Repeated demonstration of the behaviour required
Reinforcing gradual approximations of a behaviour
Removal of previously earned reinforcers as a consequence of negative behaviour

correct_answer.text: Reinforcing gradual approximations of a behaviour

questions.explanation:
Shaping: This is a form of operant conditioning where a desirable behaviour pattern is learnt by the successive reinforcement of behaviours
closer to the desired one. This is used in training animals in circus where the dog is reinforced when it runs towards the circle, then when it
jumps near the circle, then when it jumps through the circle and at last when it jumps through the circle of �re. This is also called successive
approximation.

questions.question_text: Most patients engage in certain subtle behaviours while in a fearful situation that serve to maintain the fear. These behaviours are called
questions.explanation:
In-situation safety behaviours (Salkovskis) refer to a variety of subtle behaviours/internal mental processes that most patients engage in
while in a fearful situation. These are intended to prevent feared outcome e.g., a panic disorder patient bows his head down and gently
leans leftwards when having a panic, with a hope to increase heart's circulation.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following statement is true with respect to the evidence on routine screening for dementia for all patients in primary care
settings?

options.text: Screening is found to be e�ective in primary care
Screening is clearly harmful when o�ered to elderly with no complaints
Screening is the only way of reducing the public health impact of dementia
Screening is not useful as the available tests have low sensitivity though high speci�city
Screening for dementia has insu�cient evidence in primary care attendees

correct_answer.text: Screening for dementia has insu�cient evidence in primary care attendees

questions.explanation:
The United States Preventive Services Task Force systematically reviewed the evidence and concluded that the evidence is insu�cient to
recommend for or against routine screening for dementia in older adults in primary care. The task force found good evidence that some
screening tests have good sensitivity but only fair speci�city in detecting cognitive impairment and dementia. There is fair to good evidence
that several drug therapies have a bene�cial e�ect on cognitive function, but the evidence of their bene�cial e�ects on activities of daily
living is mixed, with the bene�t being small at best. There is insu�cient evidence to determine whether the bene�ts observed in drug trials
are generalizable to patients whose disease would be detected by screening in primary care settings. The accuracy of diagnosis, the
feasibility of screening and treatment in routine clinical practice, and the potential harms of screening (for example, labeling e�ects) are also
unknown. The task force, therefore, could not determine whether the bene�ts of screening for dementia outweigh the harms. NICE has no
recommendations for screening though it advises on early recognition and referral. (Retrieved from articleid=716466)

questions.question_text: Aggression turned inward' could be a psychodynamic explanation for
questions.explanation: Aggression turned inwards cause suicidal ideas and depression. When exhibited outwards, acting out' and violent, impulsive acts result.

questions.question_text: In psychotherapy, containment is best described as

options.text: The ability of the therapist to distract the patient from distressing re-enactments
The ability of the therapist to modify and return to the patient the di�cult material in a way he can tolerate.
The ability of therapist to keep the information given to him in a con�dential manner
The capacity of the therapist to withhold the emotional content during therapeutic sessions
The capacity of the therapist to appreciate the object relationships emerging during the therapy

correct_answer.text: The ability of the therapist to modify and return to the patient the di�cult material in a way he can tolerate.

questions.explanation:
The capacity of the psychotherapist to act similar to an emotionally competent mother who interacts with her infant was termed as Alpha
function by Bion. Similiar to the mother, the alpha function allows the therapist to metabolise unbearable feelings on behalf of the patient.
These are then fed back to the patient in a form that is easy for the patient to assimilate and link with his thoughts. This process is called
containment in Bion's original sense. But later this term expanded variably, rather inaccurately referring to a capacity to hold all kinds of
anxieties on a patient's behalf. P950: Puri and Treasaden: Psychiatry: An Evidence-based text

questions.question_text:
Tom is on methadone treatment for heroin addiction. He attends A& E on two occasions saying he is running out of a supply of methadone
and demanding treatment. What is the best course of action?
questions.explanation:
It is possible that he is experiencing withdrawal symptoms, due to an inadequate dose of methadone and possibly self-medicating himself.
The best course of action is to stabilise this patient by optimizing the dose of methadone. It is inadvisable to issue additional replacement
opiates from the A&E Department. Liaising and passing on this information to the local drug service is what is essential so that they can
review their prescribing and possibly increase the daily dose with closer supervision.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a projective test of personality?
questions.explanation:
Murray was the proponent of projective personality tests though the �rst test produced was Rorschach's ink blots. Thematic Apperception
Test (Murray), Draw-a-person test, sentence completion tests are other examples.

questions.question_text: Massed practice can be used in the treatment of;
questions.explanation:
Massed negative practice is one of the most frequently used behavioral techniques in the treatment for tic disorder. The patient is asked to
deliberately perform the tic movement for speci�ed periods of time interspersed with brief periods of rest.

questions.question_text:
Sally is physically dependent on dihydrocodeine, which she is taking for back pain. She wants to stop and go back to work. What is the best
course of action?
questions.explanation:
Withdraw codeine cautiously in the �rst instance, in conjunction with other pain management approaches (e.g., pregabalin, SNRI,
psychology, TENS) and if unsuccessful then consider changing to methadone to facilitate withdrawal.

questions.question_text: Tim is taking heroin regularly. He has been tried unsuccessfully on methadone and buprenorphine. Choose next best option;
questions.explanation:
The guidelines suggest that the patient should have "speci�cally optimised higher dose oral methadone or buprenorphine maintenance
treatment" after oral maintenance therapy before moving on to injectables. Injectable heroin and methadone treatments should be
considered only for the minority of patients who are genuinely unresponsive to an optimised oral maintenance treatment approach.
Injectable and oral substitute prescribing must be supported by locally commissioned and provided mechanisms for supervised
consumption. Injectable drugs may present more risk of overdose than oral preparations and have a greater value on illicit markets and
hence may require greater levels of supervision.(Retrieved
from:www.nta.nhs.uk/uploads/nta_injectable_heroin_and_methadone_2003_fullguide.pdf)

questions.question_text:
A man who repeatedly presents to A& E with his girlfriend who is pregnant and heavy abuser of heroin. She plans to breastfeed following
childbirth. Which medication is preferable to continue if she starts breastfeeding
questions.explanation:
Methadone is considered compatible with breast-feeding. The Clinical Guidelines recommend that breast feeding should still be
encouraged, but that with regards to methadone and breast feeding "the dose is kept as low as possible while maintaining stability, and the
infant monitored to avoid sedation. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines- 316)

questions.question_text:
Which of the following drugs used to prevent relapse in alcohol use appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter
system?
questions.explanation:
Acamprosate is a synthetic taurine analogue, which appears to act centrally on glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter system. It is licensed
to prevent relapse in alcohol use and has been found to have a modest treatment e�ect.

Delirium tremens is a toxic confusional state that occurs when alcohol withdrawal symptoms are severe. The symptoms typically peak
between 72-96 hours after the last drink. The classical symptoms include confusion, distraction & clouding of consciousness, vivid
hallucinations a�ecting every sensory modality and marked tremors. Clinical features also include �eeting paranoid delusions, agitation,
sleep disturbances, signs of autonomic hyperactivity such as fever, sweating, tachycardia and hypertension

questions.question_text: Following sudden cessation of alcohol on a dependent patient, the risk of seizure is high during?
questions.explanation:
As part of alcohol withdrawal symptoms, generalized seizures rarely occur, usually within 24 hours of cessation of alcohol. Benzodiazepines
especially long-acting ones such as diazepam reduce the risk of seizures.

questions.question_text:
A man after completing his opioid detoxi�cation is highly motivated to remain on treatment and wants advice about maintaining it. Which of
the following drugs is best suited in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Naltrexone is recommended as a treatment option in detoxi�ed, formerly opioid-dependent subjects who are highly motivated to remain in
an abstinence programme. For this group, naltrexone treatment has been found by NICE to be a cost e�ective treatment strategy in aiding
abstinence from opioid misuse. (www.nice.org.uk- Technology Appraisal 115, 2007)

questions.question_text: The MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool for Treatment (MacCat-T) includes assessment of all of the following except
questions.explanation:
The MacCat-T is the product of an 8-year study of patients' capacities to make treatment decisions. It is a semi-structured interview that
assists clinicians who are conducting assessments of patients' competence to consent to treatment. It takes 20-25mins to administer and
tests the following: Understanding disorder and treatment proposed, appreciation of treatment and disorder, understanding bene�ts and
risk, �rst choice and reasoning, alternative choices, generating consequences and �nal choice. The �nal score is given in four areas:
understanding, appreciation, expressing a choice, and reasoning.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of antisocial personality among females prisoners in the UK is
questions.explanation:
Surveys of prisoners worldwide indicate a prevalence of antisocial personality disorder of 47% for men and 21% for women (Fazel & Danesh,
2002). In the UK prison population, the prevalence of people with antisocial personality disorder has been identi�ed as 63% male remand
prisoners, 49% male sentenced prisoners, and 31% female prisoners (Singleton et al., 1998). By contrast, the prevalence of psychopathy in
UK prisoners is only 4.5% using a PCL-R score of >30, and 13% using a score of >25 (Hare et al., 2000).

questions.question_text: What proportion of o�enders commit nearly 50% of all reported crime?
questions.explanation:
Repeat O�enders: In Wolfgang's famous Philadelphia cohort, about 5 percent of all o�enders in the study were responsible for more than
50 percent of the crimes. Similarly, according to the British Crime Survey, repeat victims (just over 4 percent of all victims) endure 40 percent
of the crimes reported in the survey.

questions.question_text:
You are asked to write a court report for a man convicted of a sexual assault. Which of the following is most likely to increase his risk of
further o�ending?

options.text: Two previous charges for sexual violence

correct_answer.text: Two previous charges for sexual violence

questions.explanation:
A Higher number of sex o�ences and Previous criminal history are important risk factors to increase the risk of further sexual violence in
someone who has been charged with a sexual o�ence.

questions.question_text:
A health gap
measure that includes premature mortality equivalent years of 'healthy' life lost due to disease state
questions.explanation:
Description 1 �ts proportionate mortality rate: It is a measure of contribution of a disease to societal mortality burden.
Description 2 �ts crude mortality rate: A crude rate is any rate applicable to whole population.
Case fatality rate (decription 3) is a measure of the fatal severity of the disease studied. For example, 15 patients out of 100 with anorexia

The DALY (description 4) is a health gap measure that extends the concept of potential years of life lost due to premature death (PYLL) to
include equivalent years of 'healthy' life lost in states of less than full health, broadly termed disability.

Patients with borderline personality disorder have poor self-image, unstable personal relationships, impulsive behaviour in areas such as

episodes of micro-psychosis. Feelings of chronic emptiness and fears of abandonment - termed as rejection sensitivity may lead to

Patients with schizotypal personality disorder (in ICD10 this is classi�ed as a type of schizophrenia) appear odd or eccentric, may have
